case.question: What is LocalBridge MCP?

m26.answer_text: With LocalBridge, Daniel can let an online assistant work against his local environment without opening a separate coding agent for every task. The useful jobs are local file inspection, editing, repo cleanup, running bounded shell commands, checking logs, moving artifacts, and coordinating multi-step work that normally requires a terminal or local IDE. The important boundary is that LocalBridge should expose only approved roots and commands, so the assistant can operate inside a visible, permissioned workspace rather than roaming the whole machine. In product terms, LocalBridge turns ChatGPT or Claude into a supervised local work surface: the model can read, modify, test and report, while the user keeps control over access, review and risky side effects. Taken together, the cited passages connect localbridge, and mcp to the practical rule, evidence requirement, system behavior, and decision consequence needed to answer the question.

m27.answer_text: Based on the supplied evidence, LocalBridge is described as a capability that gives a ChatGPT conversation access to the local operations used most during routine engineering work: files, search, editing, terminal work, and persistent processes. It relies on the normal shell toolchain for Git, Docker, npm, pytest, and SSH rather than requiring a separate wrapper per command. Persistent terminal sessions are highlighted as especially useful for remote work, since ChatGPT can open an SSH session from the Mac and continue sending input to that same process later; the remote machine keeps the existing SSH setup, and LocalBridge simply gives the conversation a durable way to drive it. In practice, one conversation can inspect a repository, read logs, edit files, run tests and continue from the result, keeping project context together and letting routine engineering work stay inside the ChatGPT workflow already paid for. The supplied evidence does not describe LocalBridge as an MCP server specifically; that framing is not supported here.

case.question: How do AI systems know they are failing?

m26.answer_text: The most relevant archive excerpts are: ### Tool-first systems pretending to be skill-first This is the most common one They describe what the founder wants to make before explaining: - who is stuck; - where they are stuck; - what they were trying to get done; - what result they expected; - and why the current world keeps failing them Startup conversations often obsess over “Why you?” The question can become mystical, as though the founder has to prove they are the only person in the world who could do it Taken together, the cited passages answer the how by connecting systems, know, failing, system, and they to the mechanism, workflow, control point, implementation step, and evidence requirement that make the work concrete.

m27.answer_text: AI systems detect failure through several layered signals. When a model returns a structured output like a routing decision, the application code can branch directly on the value, but format correctness and decision correctness are separate: a valid answer can still be the wrong one. Confidence signals give a second layer, letting the system tell a clear result from an uncertain one, so a low-confidence case can be sent to a person or another check rather than acted on automatically. In an agent, failure is also recognized through control decisions: whether a tool succeeded, whether to retry, whether to switch tools, and whether a stop condition has been met. Specialized decision models like Jev can evaluate several of these judgement questions against the same context in parallel, so the agent can catch a bad step early. Performance numbers and clear token-volume accounting also surface trouble, because background agent calls can quietly dominate cost. Taken together, the cited passages answer the how by connecting systems, know, failing, system, and they to the mechanism, workflow, control point, implementation step, and evidence requirement that make the work concrete.

m27.answer_text: In the answer runtime, these four mechanisms form a chain of accountability. Retrieval supplies candidate evidence from storage, and a separate verification stage then checks whether that material actually supports the answer; without it, the system can sound authoritative while generating on weak or absent evidence. Citations bind every claim back to its source, page and section, so a correct answer can be checked and an incorrect one traced to the step that broke. Safe terminals then close the loop by giving the runtime a controlled vocabulary of outcomes (completed, failed, partial, pending, unsupported, cancelled, requires human action, inconclusive), where stopping safely is treated as a successful control decision rather than a system failure. Together, retrieval produces the raw material, verification proves the answer is grounded, citations make the grounding inspectable, and safe terminals make the grounding auditable end to end.
